newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK global, non-EU trade data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK global, non-EU trade data.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to data showing a December UK global trade deficit of 845 million stg and a January non-EU trade shortfall of 398 million stg.
The Reuters consensus forecast was for a December global trade gap of 1.1 billion stg and a January non-EU deficit of 750 million vs 844 million.
"Much better than expected. What it suggests is that the deterioration we saw last month was not the first sign of sterling strength."

"Exports were better than expected in both the global and non-EU figures. The trade data has been very erratic, it's been boucing around from month to month, and it may be several months yet until we can identify the impact of sterling strength feeding through."

"The UK trade data are surprisingly good and do much to undermine recent complaints about a serious erosion of cometitiveness due to sterling strength. Export volumes to the non-EU bloc were up some 13 percent and account for a remarkably sharp narrowing in the trade deficit last month to just 398 million. The December global figures are not quite as impressive."

"The deterioration in the deficit should only come through slowly anyway as hedging activity limits the initial damage and J-curve effects help to keep nominal imports in check. Even so, these data should come as a relief and should be well received by the GBP. Not such good news for gilts, however, as the low deficit in January...implies stronger GDP."

PHILIP UGLOW, UNION PLC "In terms of the total trade figures they are relatively close to what we'd expected. But the really good news is that on the non-EU side the underlying deficit has come in very much lower than forecast. There have been concerns that we'd see the trade gap widening with the effects of sterling but what these figures may reflect is the trade gap improving because of the value effect of sterling, which means that imports will be a little cheaper and that may actually benefit the trade gap in the shorter term."
"You may well see that unwind as the months go on, but you are certainly going to see better figures for a while and then widening later in the year."
